Trigg Tromino

CountingAreaInvariants

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: cover the board around the hole with L-shaped pieces of three squares. Can you finish with no red fault lines, or with exactly two, or three?
How to play: click three squares in a row to make an L — the second click is the corner. A red line across a finished board is a fault: no piece crosses it.
Look for the math

Charles W. Trigg asked this about an 8 by 8 board with its centre four squares cut out: cover what is left with L-trominoes so that the covering has no fault line, or exactly two, or exactly three — and show that four is impossible. A fault line is a straight grid line from one side of the board to the other that no piece crosses, so one half of the tiling could slide past the other.

Why a covering exists at all

Sixty squares remain, a multiple of three. Golomb's theorem says an 8 by 8 with any one square missing can be tiled with L-trominoes. Put one tromino into the cut-out 2 by 2 so that a single square is left missing, and the theorem finishes the board. So the real question is about counting seams, not about existence.

Which lines can be faults

Label rows A–H and columns 1–8. Benjamin Schwartz proved a few short lemmas: a 2 by n strip tiles with L-trominoes only when n is a multiple of 3; two neighbouring lines cannot both be faults; a 3 by 3 cannot be tiled with L-trominoes; and a fault cannot sit next to the outer edge. Together those cut the candidates down to the three middle horizontal lines (CD, DE, EF) and the three middle vertical ones (34, 45, 56).

Zero to three, never four

Searching every L-tromino covering of this board finds 3,427 tilings. Their fault counts are 0 (1,250 of them), 1 (128), 2 (just 1), and 3 (2,048) — and none with four or more. Trigg asked for 0, 2 and 3; Schwartz also exhibited a covering with exactly one. Four is impossible for a sharper reason than the search: the only candidate set of four lines is CD, EF, 34 and 56, and that would force each corner 3 by 3 to be tiled on its own, which lemma III forbids.

Try for a covering with no red lines, then one with three. The only covering with exactly two faults (in the exhaustive search) uses the centre cross: lines DE and 45.
